summary.text: Lucas congruences and pairing the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) show that both sums vanish at \(p+r\) for \(0\le r<p\); moreover \(a(p-1)\equiv1\), while divisibility of the off-center central binomial coefficients leaves only the midpoint in \(c(p-1)\), giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Thus each Hankel matrix is anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and its determinant is the reversal-permutation sign times the \(p\)-th power of its constant anti-diagonal entry, yielding the two claimed values.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
             \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
q=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\); equivalently, all calculations may be made in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first establish the binomial congruences that will be used.

For arbitrary nonnegative integers \(N,K\), write
\[
N=N_0+pN_1,\qquad K=K_0+pK_1,
\]
where \(0\le N_0,K_0<p\). The one-digit form of Lucas's congruence says that
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom{N_0}{K_0}\binom{N_1}{K_1}\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
For completeness, this follows by comparing coefficients in \(\mathbb F_p[x]\). Since
\((1+x)^p=1+x^p\) in characteristic \(p\),
\[
(1+x)^N=(1+x)^{N_0}\bigl((1+x)^p\bigr)^{N_1}
       =(1+x)^{N_0}(1+x^p)^{N_1}.
\]
To obtain the coefficient of \(x^{K_0+pK_1}\), the first factor must contribute degree \(K_0\), because its degree is less than \(p\), and the second must contribute degree \(pK_1\). This gives (1).

We shall need the following immediate consequences. If \(0\le r<p\), then for \(0\le k_0\le r\),
\[
\binom{p+r}{k_0}\equiv \binom r{k_0},\qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+k_0}\equiv \binom r{k_0}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the base-\(p\) digits of \(p+r\) are \((r,1)\), while those of \(k_0\) and \(p+k_0\) are respectively \((k_0,0)\) and \((k_0,1)\). On the other hand, if
\[
r<k<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv0, \tag{3}
\]
because the low-digit factor supplied by (1) is \(\binom rk=0\).

We also use
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\qquad(0\le k\le p-1). \tag{4}
\]
One proof is by induction using Pascal's identity. For \(1\le k<p\), the prime \(p\) divides \(\binom pk\), and
\[
\binom pk=\binom{p-1}{k-1}+\binom{p-1}{k}.
\]
Thus modulo \(p\),
\( inom{p-1}{k}=-\binom{p-1}{k-1}\). Starting with
\(\binom{p-1}{0}=1\) gives (4).

Two congruences involving central binomial coefficients will also be important. If \(0\le m<p\) and \(p\le2m\), then
\[
\binom{2m}{m}\equiv0. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the base-\(p\) expansion of \(2m\) is
\((2m-p)+p\), whereas that of \(m\) is simply \(m\). Since
\(2m-p<m\), the low-digit factor in (1) is
\(\binom{2m-p}{m}=0\).

For every \(0\le m<p\), we furthermore have
\[
\binom{2(p+m)}{p+m}\equiv2\binom{2m}{m}. \tag{6}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2m<p\), the base-\(p\) digits of \(2(p+m)=2p+2m\) are \((2m,2)\), and those of \(p+m\) are \((m,1)\). Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{2(p+m)}{p+m}\equiv
\binom{2m}{m}\binom21=2\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
If \(2m\ge p\), the right side vanishes by (5). The left side vanishes as well: now
\[
2(p+m)=3p+(2m-p),
\]
and the low digit \(2m-p\) is smaller than the low digit \(m\) of \(p+m\). This proves (6) in both cases.

We next evaluate the relevant values of \(a\).

**Vanishing of \(a(p+r)\).** Let \(0\le r<p\). In the sum defining \(a(p+r)\), partition the indices \(0,1,\ldots,p+r\) into
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,r\},\qquad
\{r+1,\ldots,p-1\},\qquad
\{p,p+1,\ldots,p+r\}.
\]
The middle group contributes zero modulo \(p\) by (3). Pair each index \(k_0\) in the first group with \(p+k_0\) in the last group. By (2), the fourth powers of the two binomial coefficients are congruent. Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+k_0}=-(-1)^{k_0}.
\]
Consequently the two paired summands cancel. Hence
\[
a(p+r)\equiv0\qquad(0\le r<p). \tag{7}
\]

**The value of \(a(p-1)\).** By (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(p\) terms in this alternating sum, and \(p\) is odd, so the sum is \(1\). Thus
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1. \tag{8}
\]

We now establish the corresponding facts for \(c\).

**Vanishing of \(c(p+r)\).** Again let \(0\le r<p\), and denote the summand of \(c(p+r)\) at the index \(k\) by
\[
F(k)=(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^2\binom{2k}{k}
     \binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}.
\]
As before, if \(r<k<p\), then \(F(k)\equiv0\) by (3). It remains to pair \(k_0\) with \(p+k_0\) for each \(0\le k_0\le r\).

Set
\[
m=r-k_0.
\]
Then both \(k_0\) and \(m\) lie between \(0\) and \(p-1\). For the first index, we have
\[
p+r-k_0=p+m.
\]
Using (2) and then (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(k_0)
&\equiv(-1)^{k_0}\binom r{k_0}^2
       \binom{2k_0}{k_0}\binom{2(p+m)}{p+m}\\
&\equiv2(-1)^{k_0}\binom r{k_0}^2
       \binom{2k_0}{k_0}\binom{2m}{m}. \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the paired index, note that
\[
p+r-(p+k_0)=m.
\]
Again using (2) and (6), now on the central binomial coefficient associated with \(p+k_0\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(p+k_0)
&\equiv(-1)^{p+k_0}\binom r{k_0}^2
       \binom{2(p+k_0)}{p+k_0}\binom{2m}{m}\\
&\equiv-2(-1)^{k_0}\binom r{k_0}^2
       \binom{2k_0}{k_0}\binom{2m}{m}. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (9) and (10) cancel. Together with the vanishing of all middle terms, this proves
\[
c(p+r)\equiv0\qquad(0\le r<p). \tag{11}
\]

**The value of \(c(p-1)\).** Using (4), the squared binomial factor in the definition of \(c(p-1)\) becomes \(1\):
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}^2\equiv \bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^2=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
c(p-1)\equiv
\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}. \tag{12}
\]
We claim that every term except the one at \(k=q=(p-1)/2\) vanishes. If \(k>q\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so the first central binomial coefficient vanishes by (5). If \(k<q\), put \(m=p-1-k\). Then \(m<p\) and \(2m\ge p\), so the second central binomial coefficient vanishes by (5). This proves the claim.

At \(k=q\), one has \(p-1-q=q\) and \(2q=p-1\). Hence the sole surviving term in (12) is
\[
(-1)^q\binom{p-1}{q}^2.
\]
By (4), \(\binom{p-1}{q}\equiv(-1)^q\), whose square is \(1\). Thus
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^q. \tag{13}
\]

It remains to convert these sequence congruences into determinant congruences. We use a general anti-triangular Hankel determinant observation.

Let \(R\) be any commutative ring, let \(n\ge0\), and let \(s(0),s(1),\ldots\) be elements of \(R\) such that
\[
s(t)=0\qquad\text{for every }t\ge n.
\]
Consider the \(n\times n\) matrix
\[
H=(s(i+j))_{0\le i,j<n}.
\]
Then
\[
\det H=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}s(n-1)^n. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, in the determinant expansion, a permutation \(\sigma\) can give a nonzero term only if
\[
i+\sigma(i)\le n-1
\]
for every \(i\), since otherwise the corresponding matrix entry is zero. But
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\bigl(i+\sigma(i)\bigr)
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sigma(i)
=n(n-1).
\]
This is also the sum of the \(n\) upper bounds \(n-1\). Thus every inequality must be an equality:
\[
i+\sigma(i)=n-1\quad\text{for all }i.
\]
The only potentially nonzero permutation is therefore the reversing permutation
\(\sigma(i)=n-1-i\). Every factor in its product is \(s(n-1)\), and the reversing permutation has one inversion for each pair of distinct indices, hence \(n(n-1)/2\) inversions. This proves (14).

Now let \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) be any integer sequence satisfying
\[
g(p+r)\equiv0\qquad(0\le r<p). \tag{15}
\]
In \(\mathbb F_p\), define a truncated sequence
\[
s(t)=
\begin{cases}
g(t)\bmod p,&t<p,\\0,&t\ge p.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(0\le i,j<p\), the sum \(i+j\) is at most \(2p-2\). If \(i+j<p\), then by definition \(s(i+j)\) is the residue of \(g(i+j)\). If \(i+j\ge p\), write
\(i+j=p+r\), where \(0\le r\le p-2<p\); then (15) says that the residue of \(g(i+j)\) is zero, again equal to \(s(i+j)\). Thus reducing the Hankel matrix \((g(i+j))\) entrywise modulo \(p\) produces exactly the matrix \((s(i+j))\).

Applying (14) with \(n=p\), and using the fact that reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with the determinant, yields
\[
\det(g(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}g(p-1)^p. \tag{16}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd and \(q=(p-1)/2\),
\[
(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=(-1)^{pq}=(-1)^q. \tag{17}
\]
Consequently (16) becomes
\[
\det(g(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^q g(p-1)^p. \tag{18}
\]

Apply (18) first to \(g=a\). Condition (15) is exactly (7), and (8) gives \(a(p-1)\equiv1\). Therefore
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^q\cdot1^p
=(-1)^q
=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}.
\]

Finally apply (18) to \(g=c\). Condition (15) follows from (11), while (13) says that \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^q\). Hence
\[
\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^q\bigl((-1)^q\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, an odd power of \((-1)^q\) is again \((-1)^q\). The last expression is therefore
\[
(-1)^q(-1)^q=(-1)^{2q}=1.
\]
This proves both asserted determinant congruences.
